title: Ordinary Time, lived
hook: the long green season for growing
tomorrow: if Lent had a plan, how many things would be on it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, chalk over the door: the house blessed, and blessed again next year. Now the decorations come down, and the long stretch begins.

Three weeks into a new workout, the mirror looks exactly the same. Same with a language app, a new instrument, a friendship you're trying to rebuild: the feeling is that nothing's happening. The Church has a whole season for that feeling. After Christmas, and again after Pentecost, the priest's vestments turn green and the calendar settles into Ordinary Time: numbered weeks, fewer big feasts, Sunday after Sunday after Sunday.
screen: `THE MIRROR LOOKS THE SAME.` → `THE VESTMENTS TURN GREEN.` → `SUNDAY AFTER SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: The question is old: how does anything actually grow? Mark's Gospel gives Jesus's answer in a short parable. A man scatters seed, then sleeps and rises, night and day, and the seed springs up while he doesn't know how. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "For the earth of itself bringeth forth fruit, first the blade, then the ear, afterwards the full corn in the ear." First, then, afterwards. Growth comes in an order you can't skip, and most of it happens while you're not watching. Green is the color for that: a field in midsummer, nothing to photograph, everything working. That's the Catholic case for ordinary weeks. You grow by showing up, Sunday after Sunday, a few verses at a time. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. In Pirkei Avot, the Jewish collection of the sayings of the sages, Rabbi Tarfon says the day is short and the work is great, and then: it isn't on you to finish the work, but you aren't free to walk away from it either. Shared ground: growth is slow, and you keep at it. One honest difference: Mark's parable leans on what grows while the farmer sleeps, a gift he can't explain. Tarfon's saying leans on the worker who keeps coming back to the task. One watches the field; the other keeps working it.
screen: `HOW DOES ANYTHING GROW?` · `FIRST THE BLADE, THEN THE EAR.` · `GREEN: EVERYTHING WORKING.` · `TARFON: DON'T WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `GROW SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper and write one thing you'd like to grow this season, small enough to tend each week: patience with a sibling, ten minutes of reading, a friendship. Under it, write only the next step, the blade, not the full ear. Then sit with the paper in your hands, and keep it somewhere you'll see it on an ordinary day.
Ordinary Time. The long green season of numbered weeks, for growing the way seed grows.
Here's the line: grow slowly, first the blade, then the ear, and no skipping ahead. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Ordinary Time, Catholic priests wear green and the Sunday Gospels move through one Gospel week by week; Catholics live it by keeping Sunday Mass and daily prayer through the long stretches between feasts.

chat.says: hannah's dad, at her house: 'you don't have to finish the work, but you can't quit it.' is that ours?
options: It's Rabbi Tarfon, in Pirkei Avot. Close to Mark's seed: grow slowly. Different book.
Yes, that's Mark's line: Jesus says it in his parable of the growing seed.
Doesn't matter whose. Every religion says exactly this, word for word.
chat.meaning: Rabbi Tarfon's saying in Pirkei Avot shares ground with Mark's seed parable: growth is slow and you keep at it. Each belongs to its own tradition.
